rw: The ACA individual mandate required most people to hold health coverage or pay a tax penalty, and Congress reduced that penalty to zero beginning in 2019.

ww.A requirement to buy drugs from a pharma: The individual mandate concerned holding health insurance coverage, not where a patient buys drugs, and the ACA set no rule tying prescriptions to a local pharmacy.
ww.A requirement to see a doctor each year: The mandate never required annual check-ups; preventive visits are a covered benefit patients may choose to use, while the mandate itself only concerned holding insurance coverage.
ww.A requirement to work for a set number o: Work hour requirements belong to some Medicaid rules, not the individual mandate, which only required people to carry health insurance coverage or pay a penalty.

rw: Certificate of need is a state process requiring providers to win approval before building, expanding or buying major equipment, which aims to limit duplicated services and rising costs.

ww.A drug approval that lets a company sell: Approval to sell a new drug comes from the FDA through its drug review, which is a separate federal process and has nothing to do with certificate of need.
ww.A staff license that lets a person work: A nurse or doctor is licensed by a state board, which grants personal practice permission, whereas certificate of need applies to facilities and projects instead of individual workers.
ww.A patient permission slip that is signed: A signed patient permission slip describes informed consent for a procedure, which is an individual patient matter and not the state facility approval known as certificate of need.

rw: A state medical license is the official permission a state board grants a physician to practice medicine within that state, after meeting education, exam and character requirements.

ww.A drug approval given to a new medicine: Drug approval for new medicines is granted by the FDA, which is a federal agency, while a state medical license is permission given to a physician to practice.
ww.A hospital permit that lets a building b: A hospital permit is a facility license for a building, but a state medical license is granted to an individual physician rather than to any building.
ww.A billing number that names a provider o: A billing number such as an NPI identifies a provider on claims, but it does not give legal permission to practice medicine, which a license does.

rw: Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, patients generally have a right to inspect their records and obtain copies, with limited exceptions such as some psychotherapy notes.

ww.Patients cannot see their records, as th: HIPAA gives patients a right to see their records, so the claim that the hospital owns them and bars patients from viewing them is wrong.
ww.Only doctors can see them, and patients: HIPAA does not limit record access to doctors, because patients are given a right to inspect and get copies of their own records.
ww.Records belong to the public and anyone: Medical records are protected health information under HIPAA, so they are not public property and strangers cannot demand to read them without proper authorization.

rw: The Patient Self-Determination Act requires facilities that receive Medicare or Medicaid funds to tell patients about their rights to make decisions and to use advance directives.

ww.A law on billing that tells hospitals ho: Billing rules are set by other laws and payer contracts, while the Patient Self-Determination Act is about informing patients of their rights to accept or refuse treatment.
ww.A law on drug prices that limits what ph: The Act has nothing to do with pharmacy drug price limits; it concerns patient rights, not what pharmacies charge for medicine across the country.
ww.A law on staffing that sets the number o: Nurse staffing ratios are set by state laws or hospital policy, not by the Patient Self-Determination Act, which is about patient decision rights.

rw: The Controlled Substances Act sets federal rules for manufacturing, distributing and dispensing drugs with abuse potential, sorting them into five schedules according to risk and medical use.

ww.A law on billing that tells hospitals ho: Billing rules come from other laws, whereas the Controlled Substances Act regulates the making, distribution and possession of drugs that have a potential for abuse.
ww.A law on hospital staffing that sets how: Nurse staffing levels are not covered by the Controlled Substances Act, which deals with drug control and not with how many nurses work on a ward.
ww.A law on privacy that decides who may re: Patient record privacy is governed by HIPAA, not the Controlled Substances Act, which concerns drugs that carry abuse or dependence risks rather than who may read a record.

rw: Schedule I drugs have the highest abuse potential and no accepted medical use under federal law, with heroin and LSD as examples.

ww.Schedule IV: Schedule IV drugs have a low abuse potential and do have accepted medical uses, such as certain sleep and anxiety medicines, so they do not fit this description.
ww.Schedule V: Schedule V drugs have the lowest abuse potential of the scheduled groups and accepted medical uses, such as some cough preparations, so they cannot be the highest risk.
ww.Schedule III: Schedule III drugs have moderate abuse potential and accepted medical uses, such as some anabolic steroid products, so they do not match the highest risk with no medical use.

rw: Mandatory reporting is a legal duty placed on certain professionals to report situations such as suspected child abuse, elder abuse or some diseases to the proper authorities.

ww.Reporting to friends and family about th: Telling friends and family about cases breaks patient privacy, and mandatory reporting means a legal duty to report to authorities, not to private contacts.
ww.Reporting to the media about the cases o: Telling the media about patients violates confidentiality, whereas mandatory reporting sends specific legal information to designated agencies rather than to the press.
ww.Optional gossip about the cases that sta: Gossip about cases is a privacy breach and never optional, while mandatory reporting is a legal requirement that sends specific concerns to proper authorities.

rw: Active listening helps staff truly understand patient needs, concerns and instructions, which builds trust and prevents errors such as missed symptoms or misunderstood directions.

ww.It replaces documentation of the care th: Documentation is still required for care given, and listening does not replace it; active listening helps staff understand what patients need and say.
ww.It avoids patient questions so that visi: Active listening invites patient questions and does not avoid them, so it does not work to end visits quickly but to improve understanding.
ww.It shortens visits at all costs, so more: Active listening does not aim to shorten visits at any cost, since rushing causes missed information and errors that listening is meant to prevent.

rw: Empathy is the ability to understand and share another person's feelings, which helps staff connect with patients and respond to their emotional needs.

ww.Ignoring emotions and focusing only on f: Ignoring emotions to focus on tasks is the opposite of empathy, because empathy requires noticing and responding to how a person feels.
ww.Giving orders to patients and to staff o: Giving orders is a form of directing others, not empathy, which means understanding and sharing feelings instead of commanding patients or staff.
ww.Feeling sorry in pity for another person: Feeling pity is sympathy, which looks down on someone from a distance, whereas empathy means sharing and understanding the other person's feelings from their view.

rw: Plain language avoids jargon, and teach-back asks the patient to repeat instructions in their own words, which confirms real understanding for patients with low health literacy.

ww.Using medical jargon with the patient in: Medical jargon is hard for patients with low health literacy to follow, so using it in every talk would make understanding worse.
ww.Speaking quickly to save time during eac: Speaking quickly gives a patient with low health literacy less time to take in information, so it hurts understanding even if it saves time.
ww.Handing over a long form only, to be rea: A long form handed over for reading at home relies on reading skill, which a patient with low health literacy may lack, so it will not help.

rw: Cultural competence means giving care that respects patients' cultural beliefs, values and languages, so that care fits who they are and is understood.

ww.Treating all patients identically, whate: Treating everyone identically ignores differences in belief and language, so it is not cultural competence, which adapts care to each patient's background.
ww.Speaking one language only, and using it: Using only one language with every patient excludes those who speak another language, whereas cultural competence includes using interpreters and respecting language needs.
ww.Ignoring culture and treating each patie: Ignoring culture treats everyone the same way and misses beliefs that affect care, so it is the opposite of cultural competence.

rw: A qualified medical interpreter should be used when a patient has limited English proficiency, so that instructions, consent and symptoms are conveyed accurately and completely.

ww.Only for children who are treated at a c: Interpreter need depends on language ability, not age, so limiting interpreters to children misses adult patients who also cannot communicate well in English.
ww.Only for staff who work in the hospital: Interpreters serve patients and families who have language needs, not staff, so restricting them to employees misses the patients who actually need language help.
ww.Never, as patients should use their own: Relatives may misinterpret or leave out details and can compromise privacy, so qualified interpreters should be used instead of never using them or leaning on family.

rw: SBAR is a structured communication tool standing for Situation, Background, Assessment and Recommendation, used to pass clear and concise patient information between clinicians.

ww.A building plan that shows where each de: A building plan showing department locations is a floor map, whereas SBAR is a structured communication tool used by clinicians to share patient information.
ww.A drug name that nurses use when they wr: SBAR is not a drug name used for orders, since it is a communication format and has nothing to do with medications or prescriptions.
ww.A billing code that tells an insurer whi: Billing codes such as CPT identify services for insurers, but SBAR is a communication format for handing patient information between clinicians, not a code.

rw: A chain of communication problem happens when information gets lost, changed or distorted as it is passed through many people, as in a game of telephone.

ww.A supply chain that moves goods from a f: A supply chain moves goods from factories to shops, which is logistics, whereas a chain of communication problem concerns messages that become distorted along the way.
ww.A phone cord that connects an office tel: A phone cord is a physical device, not a communication problem, while a chain of communication problem concerns messages being changed as they pass between people.
ww.A billing chain that links each charge t: A billing chain linking charges to departments is an accounting idea, and it does not describe messages losing accuracy as they pass between people.

rw: Transformational leadership inspires followers with a vision so they exceed expectations, and it drives change by motivating people instead of relying on orders and rules.

ww.Managing by rules only, and giving staff: Managing by rules alone with no staff input describes a bureaucratic or autocratic style, whereas transformational leaders inspire staff with a vision and invite their ideas.
ww.Micromanaging every task and checking th: Micromanaging every task is a controlling style, but transformational leaders trust and motivate staff toward a shared vision instead of checking each step.
ww.Ignoring staff and leaving them to work: Ignoring staff and offering no support is laissez-faire neglect, while transformational leaders actively engage, motivate and develop their teams toward a vision.

rw: Servant leadership means leading by putting the needs and growth of team members first, so the leader serves the team and helps people develop and succeed.

ww.Serving food to the patients and staff i: Serving food in a cafeteria is a job, not a leadership style, whereas servant leadership means leaders put the needs of their team first.
ww.Demanding obedience from staff and givin: Demanding obedience without explaining orders is autocratic leadership, the opposite of servant leadership, which puts team needs and growth ahead of the leader's authority.
ww.Avoiding responsibility for the work and: Avoiding responsibility is poor leadership, while servant leaders accept responsibility and work to support their team so that people can do their best work.

rw: An autocratic leadership style means the leader makes decisions alone with little or no input from the team, and expects staff to follow the instructions given.

ww.The team votes on everything and the lea: A team voting on everything describes democratic leadership, where the leader counts votes, whereas an autocratic leader decides alone without seeking much input from the group.
ww.No direction at all is given to the staf: Giving no direction describes laissez-faire leadership, not autocratic, because an autocratic leader gives firm direction and issues orders.
ww.Decisions by consensus of the whole team: Decisions made by consensus of the whole team describe participative or democratic leadership, which is the opposite of an autocratic leader deciding alone.

rw: Laissez-faire leaders give team members freedom to make their own decisions with little direction, which suits skilled and self-motivated staff but can leave a team without guidance.

ww.Constant supervision of the staff by a l: Constant supervision of every task describes micromanagement, which is the opposite of laissez-faire leadership, where the leader steps back and offers little oversight.
ww.Strict control by a leader who sets ever: A leader who sets every rule and checks all work is exercising strict control, which describes an autocratic style and not a hands-off laissez-faire style.
ww.Voting on all choices, with each member: Voting on all choices describes a democratic style, while laissez-faire leaders leave decisions to team members without formal votes and give little direction.

rw: The best first step is to meet with both nurses, listen to each view and work toward a fair solution, which handles the disagreement respectfully and constructively.

ww.Post the dispute publicly so nurses can: Posting a dispute publicly invites side-taking and embarrasses staff, which makes the conflict worse instead of resolving it, so it is not a good first step.
ww.Punish both immediately and without hear: Punishing both nurses without hearing either side is unfair and ignores the facts, so it could add resentment and does nothing to solve the coverage problem.
ww.Ignore the issue and hope that it goes a: Ignoring a conflict rarely makes it disappear and may let it grow, so a manager should address it early rather than hoping it resolves itself.

rw: A code of ethics is a set of principles guiding professional conduct, helping staff decide what is right when duties, patient wishes or values come into conflict.

ww.A color code for alerts posted in the ho: A color code for alerts is an emergency signal system, not a code of ethics, which is a set of principles guiding professional behavior.
ww.A billing code that names a service on a: A billing code names a service on a claim for payment, so it concerns finances and not the moral principles that make up a code of ethics.
ww.A dress code that tells staff what to we: A dress code covers what staff wear, which is a workplace policy on appearance, whereas a code of ethics guides moral and professional conduct.

rw: Beneficence means acting in the best interest of the patient, doing good and promoting well being, which is a core principle of medical ethics.

ww.Avoiding all treatment, so that no risk: Avoiding all treatment to prevent risk would deny patients needed care, whereas beneficence means actively doing good, so it does not equal withholding care.
ww.Saving costs for the hospital each year: Saving hospital costs is a financial goal and may conflict with patient welfare, whereas beneficence concerns the patient's good rather than the hospital's savings.
ww.Following orders only, with no thought o: Following orders without thinking about care ignores patient welfare, while beneficence requires thoughtful action that aims at the good of the patient.

rw: Nonmaleficence means do no harm, so health workers must avoid actions that injure patients, and it is among the core principles of medical ethics.

ww.Do all asked: Doing everything asked would sometimes cause harm, so it is not the meaning of nonmaleficence, which sets a limit by forbidding harm to patients.
ww.Do most tasks: Doing most tasks has nothing to do with harm, so it does not capture the meaning of nonmaleficence, which concerns avoiding injury to patients.
ww.Do nothing: Doing nothing can itself harm a patient who needs care, so nonmaleficence means avoiding harm and does not mean taking no action at all.

rw: Patient autonomy is the right of the patient to make their own informed decisions about care, which is why consent and refusal must be respected.

ww.Staff decide for patients about their ca: Staff deciding for patients describes paternalism, which is the opposite of autonomy, where patients choose after receiving information about their care and options.
ww.Families decide always, whatever the wis: Families deciding regardless of the patient's wishes overrides a competent patient's own choice, which conflicts with autonomy, a patient's right to choose for themselves.
ww.The hospital decides every part of the c: A hospital deciding every part of care removes the patient's choice, and so it contradicts autonomy, which respects the patient's right to decide.

rw: Justice in medical ethics means the fair distribution of healthcare resources and treatment, so that patients are treated equitably and burdens and benefits are shared fairly.

ww.Courtroom punishment given by a judge af: Courtroom punishment is a legal idea, but justice in medical ethics is about fairness in distributing care and resources, not about trials or penalties.
ww.Treating only some people and leaving th: Treating only some people and leaving others without care is unfair, so it is the opposite of the justice principle, which requires fairness for all.
ww.Giving more care to the wealthy than to: Giving more care to the wealthy is unfair favoritism, whereas justice in medical ethics requires that resources be shared fairly, regardless of wealth.

rw: A patient advocate helps patients understand their rights, speak up and resolve concerns about their care, serving as a guide and voice inside the system.

ww.A pharmacist who fills the prescriptions: A pharmacist fills prescriptions, which is a dispensing role, whereas a patient advocate helps patients understand their rights and sort out problems with their care.
ww.A security guard who watches the doors a: A security guard protects the building and people inside, so that role is safety and not helping patients with their rights, which is advocate work.
ww.A billing collector who contacts patient: A billing collector pursues payment on unpaid accounts, which serves the hospital's finances, while a patient advocate supports patients in understanding rights and resolving concerns.

rw: Patient experience measures patients' perceptions of their care, such as communication, responsiveness and respect, usually gathered through surveys such as HCAHPS.

ww.Only staffing levels on the wards counte: Staffing levels are an operational measure of resources, not patient perception, so they do not describe what patient experience measures.
ww.Only billing and the size of the bills s: Billing amounts are a financial matter and not a measure of how patients perceive the care they received, which is what patient experience measures.
ww.Only clinical outcomes such as survival: Survival and recovery rates are clinical outcome measures, which differ from patient experience, since experience captures patients' views about communication and responsiveness.

rw: HCAHPS is a national standardized survey of hospital patients' experiences, covering things like communication with nurses and doctors, and its results are publicly reported.

ww.A staff test of skills taken by all new: A skills test for new nurses is a competency check, while HCAHPS is a standard survey that asks patients about their hospital experience.
ww.A billing code that names a service on a: A billing code names a service on a claim, but HCAHPS is a patient survey, so it is not a code of any kind.
ww.A drug schedule that lists the times for: A drug schedule lists medication times, but HCAHPS measures patient experience through a survey, so it has nothing to do with medicine timing.

rw: Root cause analysis is a structured process for finding the underlying causes of an error or adverse event, so that fixes can prevent it from recurring.

ww.Blaming an individual for the error and: Blaming an individual and penalizing them ignores system problems, whereas root cause analysis searches for underlying system causes of an error rather than seeking someone to punish.
ww.Dismissing an event as a one-off and tak: Dismissing an event as a one-off means no learning, but root cause analysis digs into why an event happened so it can be prevented.
ww.Planting trees on the grounds of the hos: Planting trees on hospital grounds is landscaping, so it has no link to the study of why errors or adverse events occur.

rw: A just culture balances accountability with learning from errors, so staff report mistakes openly and are not blamed unfairly, while reckless behavior is still addressed.

ww.Punishing all errors in the same way, wh: Punishing every error alike ignores intent and cause, so it is not a just culture, which separates honest mistakes from reckless behavior and treats each fairly.
ww.Ignoring errors that occur on the wards: Ignoring errors prevents learning and leaves risks in place, so it is not a just culture, which investigates errors to improve safety.
ww.Hiding errors from the managers and from: Hiding errors prevents learning and endangers patients, whereas a just culture encourages open reporting so that mistakes can be reviewed and corrected.

rw: An incident report is a document recording an unusual event involving a patient or staff, such as a fall or medication error, so the facts can be reviewed.

ww.A lab result that shows the levels of ch: A lab result reports chemical levels in blood, which is a clinical test report, not an incident report, which documents unusual events.
ww.A billing statement sent to a patient to: A billing statement shows charges for care and requests payment, so it is a financial document and not an incident report about an unusual event.
ww.A staff review of the work done by a nur: A yearly review of a nurse's work is a performance evaluation, and it is not an incident report, which records a specific unusual event.

rw: The suffix -ology means the study of, as in cardiology, the study of the heart, and biology, the study of life.

ww.Pain or ache: Pain or ache is expressed by the suffix -algia or -dynia, as in neuralgia, and not by -ology, which means the study of.
ww.Removal of it: Removal is expressed by the suffix -ectomy, as in appendectomy, and not by -ology, which means the study of something.
ww.Inflammation: Inflammation is expressed by the suffix -itis, as in arthritis, and not by -ology, which means the study of something.

rw: The root nephr refers to the kidney, as in nephritis, which means inflammation of the kidney, and nephrology, the study of the kidney.

ww.Stomach: The stomach is named by the root gastr, as in gastric, whereas nephr refers to the kidney, so stomach is not the answer.
ww.Heart: The heart is named by the root cardi, as in cardiology, and not by nephr, which refers to the kidney.
ww.Liver: The liver is named by the root hepat, as in hepatitis, and not by nephr, which refers to the kidney.

rw: The root neur refers to a nerve, as in neurology, the study of the nervous system, and neuralgia, which means nerve pain.

ww.Bone: Bone is named by the root oste, as in osteoporosis, whereas neur refers to a nerve, so bone is not the answer.
ww.Muscle: Muscle is named by the root my or myo, as in myalgia, and not by neur, which refers to a nerve.
ww.Skin: Skin is named by the root derm, as in dermatology, and not by neur, which refers to a nerve.

rw: The root oste refers to bone, as in osteoporosis, a condition of weak bones, and osteoarthritis, which is joint disease with bone changes.

ww.Blood: Blood is named by the root hem or hemat, as in hematology, and not by oste, which refers to bone.
ww.Skin: Skin is named by the root derm, as in dermatitis, and not by oste, which refers to bone.
ww.Nerve: Nerve is named by the root neur, as in neuropathy, and not by oste, which refers to bone.

rw: The root derm refers to skin, as in dermatology, the study of skin, and dermatitis, which means inflammation of the skin.

ww.Eye: Eye is named by the root ophthalm or ocul, as in ophthalmology, and not by derm, which refers to skin.
ww.Heart: Heart is named by the root cardi, as in cardiology, and not by derm, which refers to skin.
ww.Bone: Bone is named by the root oste, as in osteitis, and not by derm, which refers to skin.

rw: The root gastr refers to the stomach, as in gastritis, which is inflammation of the stomach, and gastroenterology, the study of the digestive tract.

ww.Liver: Liver is named by the root hepat, as in hepatitis, and not by gastr, which refers to the stomach.
ww.Lung: Lung is named by the root pulmon or pneumon, as in pulmonary, and not by gastr, which refers to the stomach.
ww.Brain: Brain is named by the root cerebr or encephal, as in encephalitis, and not by gastr, which refers to the stomach.

rw: Tachycardia means an abnormally fast heart rate, usually above 100 beats per minute at rest, from tachy for fast and cardia for heart.

ww.A normal heart rate today: A normal heart rate is not tachycardia, because the root tachy means fast, so tachycardia means an abnormally fast heart rate instead of a normal one.
ww.No heartbeat at all in the heart: No heartbeat is called asystole or cardiac arrest, whereas tachycardia means a fast heart rate, so the heart is still beating.
ww.A slow heart rate below sixty: A slow heart rate below sixty is bradycardia, from brady for slow, and so it is the opposite of tachycardia, which is fast.

rw: Bradycardia means an abnormally slow heart rate, usually under 60 beats per minute at rest, from brady for slow and cardia for heart.

ww.A normal heart rate today: A normal heart rate is not bradycardia, because brady means slow, so bradycardia refers to an abnormally slow heart rate instead of a normal one.
ww.No heartbeat at all in the heart: No heartbeat is asystole or cardiac arrest, whereas bradycardia means a slow heart rate, which means the heart is still beating.
ww.A fast heart rate above a hundred: A fast heart rate above a hundred is tachycardia, from tachy for fast, and it is the opposite of bradycardia, which is slow.

rw: Dyspnea means difficult or labored breathing, from dys for difficult or painful and pnea for breathing, and patients often describe it as shortness of breath.

ww.Normal breathing at rest in adults: Normal breathing is called eupnea, from eu for good, and not dyspnea, which refers to breathing that is difficult or labored.
ww.Fast breathing at rest or in sleep: Fast breathing is called tachypnea, from tachy for fast, and not dyspnea, which refers to difficult or labored breathing.
ww.No breathing at all in the patient: No breathing at all is called apnea, from a for without, and not dyspnea, which refers to difficult or labored breathing.

rw: A hematoma is a collection of blood outside blood vessels, such as a bruise or a larger pool of blood under the skin or in tissue.

ww.A skin rash that appears on the arms and: A skin rash is an eruption of the skin, whereas a hematoma is a collection of blood, from hemat for blood and oma for mass.
ww.A tumor of bone found by an X-ray scan: A tumor of bone is an osteoma, from oste for bone and oma, and a hematoma involves blood, not bone.
ww.A heart murmur heard through a stethosco: A heart murmur is a sound heard with a stethoscope, whereas a hematoma is a pool of blood in the tissue that forms after a vessel leaks.

rw: NPO stands for nil per os, a Latin phrase meaning nothing by mouth, an order given before surgery or tests so the stomach is empty.

ww.Needs pain overview: Needs pain overview is not a real meaning of NPO, which is a Latin abbreviation, nil per os, meaning nothing by mouth.
ww.Normal patient care: Normal patient care is not what NPO stands for, since it comes from the Latin nil per os and means nothing by mouth.
ww.Nurse patient order: Nurse patient order is an invented expansion, because NPO comes from the Latin nil per os, meaning that the patient may take nothing by mouth.

rw: STAT comes from the Latin statim and means immediately, so a STAT order must be carried out at once, usually in an emergency or urgent situation.

ww.Sometime today: Sometime today is far too loose for STAT, which comes from the Latin statim and means to act immediately, with no delay.
ww.Statistics: STAT does not mean statistics, since it comes from the Latin statim, meaning immediately, and it flags an order that must be done at once.
ww.Standard time: Standard time suggests ordinary routine timing, but STAT comes from statim and signals urgency, meaning the order must be carried out immediately.

rw: PRN comes from the Latin pro re nata and means as needed, so a PRN medication is given only when the patient requires it, such as for pain.

ww.After surgery: After surgery is not what PRN means, since it comes from the Latin pro re nata, meaning as needed, and it has no link to surgery timing.
ww.Before meals: Before meals is abbreviated AC, from ante cibum, and not PRN, which comes from the Latin pro re nata and means as needed.
ww.Every night: Every night is abbreviated QHS or HS, and not PRN, which means as needed and carries no fixed schedule.

rw: BID stands for the Latin bis in die, meaning twice a day, so a BID medicine is taken two times in each day, often morning and evening.

ww.Four a day: Four a day is abbreviated QID, from quater in die, and not BID, which stands for bis in die, meaning twice a day.
ww.Three a day: Three a day is abbreviated TID, from ter in die, and not BID, which stands for bis in die, meaning twice a day.
ww.Once a day: Once a day is abbreviated QD or daily, and not BID, which stands for bis in die, meaning twice a day.

rw: TID stands for the Latin ter in die, which means three times a day, so a TID medicine is given three times in each day.

ww.Twice a day only: Twice a day is abbreviated BID, from bis in die, and not TID, which stands for ter in die, meaning three times a day.
ww.Once a day only: Once a day is abbreviated QD or daily, and not TID, which stands for ter in die, meaning three times a day.
ww.Four times a day: Four times a day is abbreviated QID, from quater in die, and not TID, which stands for ter in die, meaning three times a day.

rw: U for units is on the Joint Commission's Do Not Use list because it can be mistaken for 0, 4 or cc, causing overdoses, so units should be written out.

ww.BP, which is used for blood pressure rea: BP is a standard abbreviation for blood pressure that is widely used and is not on the Do Not Use list, which names error-prone shorthand.
ww.mg, the standard abbreviation for millig: The abbreviation mg for milligrams is standard and accepted, and it is not on the Do Not Use list, which names only error-prone abbreviations.
ww.mL, which is used to show a volume in mi: The abbreviation mL for milliliters is standard and accepted, and it is not on the Do Not Use list, which names only error-prone abbreviations.

rw: Vital signs are measurements of basic body functions, namely temperature, pulse, respiration and blood pressure, and they give a quick picture of a patient's health.

ww.Billing codes that describe the services: Billing codes describe services for insurers, and they are not vital signs, which are measurements of the body's basic functions taken at each visit.
ww.Patient names and dates of birth that ar: Names and birth dates identify the patient and are not vital signs, which are measurements of basic body function, such as pulse and temperature.
ww.Laboratory results that are collected fr: Laboratory results come from tests of blood and other specimens, and they are not vital signs, which are quick bedside measurements of basic body function.

rw: A normal adult resting pulse ranges from 60 to 100 beats per minute, and below 60 is bradycardia while above 100 is tachycardia.

ww.120 to 160 beats a minute: A pulse of 120 to 160 beats a minute is tachycardia in an adult at rest, so it is far above the normal range.
ww.20 to 40 beats a minute: A pulse of 20 to 40 beats a minute is severe bradycardia, far below the normal adult resting range of 60 to 100.
ww.200 to 250 beats a minute: A pulse of 200 to 250 beats a minute is dangerously fast and far above the normal adult resting range of 60 to 100.

rw: A typical normal adult body temperature is about 98.6 degrees F, or 37 degrees C, though healthy people vary slightly around this figure.

ww.About 88°F or less: A temperature of about 88 degrees F or less is severe hypothermia, which is a medical emergency and far below normal.
ww.About 108°F or more: A temperature of about 108 degrees F or more is a life threatening hyperpyrexia, far above the normal body temperature of about 98.6 degrees F.
ww.About 78°F or less: A temperature of about 78 degrees F or less is extreme hypothermia, far below the normal body temperature of about 98.6 degrees F.

rw: A blood pressure reading of 120/80 represents systolic pressure over diastolic pressure, measured in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg), the pressure when the heart beats and rests.

ww.Height over weight in feet and inches: Height and weight are body measurements, but a reading of 120/80 is blood pressure, so the number is not a height over weight ratio.
ww.Pulse over respiration at the bedside: Pulse and respiration are other vital signs, but they are not written as a fraction; 120/80 is a blood pressure reading.
ww.Age over weight in years and in pounds o: Age and weight are not written as a fraction in a reading, since 120/80 is a blood pressure measured in mm Hg, not age over weight.

rw: The first step in check-in is verifying the patient's identity and insurance information, which ensures the right chart is used and that billing is correct later.

ww.Sending the bill to the insurer or the p: Sending the bill comes after care is delivered, so it cannot be the first step at check-in, which starts with confirming who the patient is.
ww.Ordering tests of the blood and other fl: Ordering tests of blood and other fluids happens during care, after check-in and the provider's assessment, so it cannot be the first step of check-in.
ww.Discharging the patient after the treatm: Discharging the patient happens at the end of the visit, so it cannot be the first step of the check-in process.

rw: The chief complaint records the main reason the patient is seeking care, ideally in the patient's own words, and it guides the rest of the visit.

ww.To record staff concerns about the work: Staff concerns about work and hours are an employment matter and not recorded in a chief complaint, which captures the reason the patient came.
ww.To record billing disputes between a pat: Billing disputes are handled by the business office and are not documented as a chief complaint, which records why the patient is seeking care.
ww.To record insurance details such as the: Insurance details are registration data and not the chief complaint, which states the main reason the patient is seeking care.

rw: SOAP stands for Subjective, Objective, Assessment and Plan, a standard format for organizing clinical notes so that information is recorded in a consistent order.

ww.Staff, Office, Admin and Policy headings: Staff, Office, Admin and Policy are not SOAP headings; SOAP is a clinical note format with sections for the patient's findings and plan.
ww.Sign, Order, Act, Pay for the care: Sign, Order, Act and Pay do not describe a clinical note; SOAP stands for Subjective, Objective, Assessment and Plan.
ww.Scan, Open, Add, Print for the chart: Scan, Open, Add and Print describe office computer tasks and not a clinical note; SOAP stands for Subjective, Objective, Assessment and Plan.

rw: The Subjective section records what the patient says, such as symptoms, history and complaints, in the patient's own description of how they feel.

ww.Assessment: The Assessment section holds the provider's diagnosis or impression after reviewing the findings, not the patient's own description of symptoms, which is the subjective part.
ww.Objective: The Objective section holds measurable findings such as vital signs, exam results and labs, not the patient's own description of symptoms, which is subjective.
ww.Plan only: The Plan section lists the treatment and follow up steps, so it does not contain the patient's description of symptoms, which belongs in the Subjective section.

rw: The Objective section includes measurable data such as vital signs, physical exam findings and lab results, which are facts that can be observed or measured.

ww.Plan only: The Plan section lists treatment and follow up steps, so it does not hold lab results or vital signs, which are objective findings.
ww.Subjective: The Subjective section holds what the patient reports, so lab results and vital signs, which are measured data, do not belong there.
ww.Assessment: The Assessment section holds the provider's diagnosis or impression, so lab results and vital signs, which are measured data, are listed elsewhere.

rw: Double booking means scheduling more than one patient in the same time slot, which is sometimes used to allow for no shows but can cause long waits.

ww.Booking a room twice for cleaning so it: Booking a room twice for cleaning is a facilities matter and not the scheduling term double booking, which concerns patients sharing a time slot.
ww.Booking two offices at the same time for: Booking two offices for the same doctor is not double booking, which means placing more than one patient into the same appointment time slot.
ww.Booking staff only, with no patients put: Booking staff with no patients is not double booking, which describes more than one patient assigned to the same appointment time.

rw: Alphabetic filing arranges records by last name, then first name, in alphabet order, so a record is found by looking up the patient's name.

ww.Numeric filing: Numeric filing arranges records by assigned numbers, not by name, so it is not the system that sorts by last name.
ww.Geographic filing: Geographic filing arranges records by location such as city or region, not by last name, so it does not match the description.
ww.Chronological filing: Chronological filing arranges records by date, not by last name, so it does not match a system that sorts by patient surname.

rw: A numeric filing system files records by assigned numbers, such as a chart number given to each patient, and it needs an index to find a name.

ww.Records filed by color of the folder: Folder color is used in color coded systems and not in a numeric system, which arranges records by assigned numbers.
ww.Records filed by date of the visit: Filing by date of visit is chronological filing, not numeric filing, which arranges records by assigned numbers.
ww.Records filed by name of the patient: Filing by patient name is alphabetic filing, not numeric filing, which arranges records by assigned numbers instead of names.

rw: Medical records are retained according to state and federal laws and organizational policy, which set minimum retention periods that vary by record type and patient age.

ww.Until the patient leaves the hospital af: Records must be kept for far longer than the hospital stay, because laws set minimum retention periods, so discharge is not the end point.
ww.Not at all, as records can be thrown awa: Records cannot be discarded once the visit ends, because laws and policies require them to be kept for a set number of years.
ww.One week after the patient has been seen: One week is far too short, since laws set retention periods measured in years, so records must be kept much longer than that.

rw: The correct method is to draw a single line through the error, write the correction, then date and initial it, so the original stays readable.

ww.Tear out the page and replace it with a: Tearing out a page destroys part of the legal record, so it is not allowed; errors are corrected by a visible, dated and initialed correction.
ww.Use correction fluid to hide the error s: Correction fluid hides the original entry, which makes the record look altered, so it is not allowed in a legal medical record.
ww.Erase and rewrite the entry so that nobo: Erasing hides the original entry and may look like tampering, so it is not allowed; the original must stay readable after a correction.

rw: Aseptic technique means practices that prevent contamination by microorganisms, such as hand hygiene, sterile gloves and clean fields, so that infection is kept away from patients.

ww.Skipping hand washing before and after t: Skipping hand washing spreads germs and is the opposite of aseptic technique, which uses hand hygiene to keep microorganisms away from patients.
ww.Using dirty gloves for each patient on t: Using dirty gloves spreads microorganisms from one patient to another, which is the opposite of aseptic technique, where clean or sterile items are used.
ww.Using any tools that are at hand, whethe: Using any tool whether clean or not spreads germs, and it is the opposite of aseptic technique, which requires clean or sterile equipment.

rw: Hand hygiene is the single most effective way to prevent the spread of infection, because hands carry germs between patients, and washing or sanitizing removes them.

ww.Wearing jewelry: Wearing jewelry can trap germs and make cleaning hands harder, so it raises the risk of spreading infection instead of preventing it.
ww.Shared tools: Shared tools can pass germs from patient to patient unless cleaned between uses, so they raise infection risk rather than lower it.
ww.Skipping gloves: Skipping gloves removes a barrier between the worker and body fluids, so it raises the risk of infection instead of preventing it.

rw: Standard precautions are basic infection control practices applied to all patients, regardless of diagnosis, including hand hygiene, gloves and safe sharps handling.

ww.Precautions for only some patients with: Standard precautions apply to all patients and not only those with a known infection, because many carriers show no signs, so this answer is too narrow.
ww.Rules for billing patients and insurers: Billing rules are financial and have nothing to do with infection control, which is the purpose of standard precautions.
ww.Rules for scheduling staff shifts on the: Shift scheduling is an administrative task and has nothing to do with infection control, which is the purpose of standard precautions.

rw: PPE is gear such as gloves, masks, gowns and eye protection that protects workers from hazards like infectious material, chemicals and splashes.

ww.A billing form that a provider sends to: A billing form is sent to an insurer to request payment, and it is not protective gear, which is what PPE means.
ww.A type of insurance that pays for the co: PPE is physical equipment worn by workers, not an insurance product, so a type of insurance paying for care of hospital staff is wrong.
ww.A staff schedule that lists the shifts f: A staff schedule lists shifts and is an administrative document, so it is not personal protective equipment, which is gear worn for safety.

rw: A sharps container is a puncture resistant, leak proof container for safely disposing of needles and other sharp objects, which protects workers from needle stick injuries.

ww.Storing money in the cash office of a ho: A sharps container is a puncture resistant box for used needles, not a place to store money in a cash office.
ww.Storing food for staff in the hospital k: Food is not stored in a sharps container, which is a puncture resistant box for used needles, since food would be unsafe near sharps.
ww.Storing records of patients in the files: Patient records are stored in files or electronic systems, not in a sharps container, which is made to hold used needles safely.

rw: A Safety Data Sheet describes the hazards of a chemical and how to handle, store, and respond to spills or exposure with it safely.

ww.A staff roster that lists who works on w: A staff roster lists who works which shift and is a scheduling document, not a Safety Data Sheet, which describes chemical hazards.
ww.A patient chart that lists the diagnoses: A patient chart lists diagnoses and treatments, which is a clinical record, and it is not a Safety Data Sheet, which describes chemical hazards.
ww.A billing form that a provider sends to: A billing form requests insurer payment, so it is a financial document and not a Safety Data Sheet, which describes chemical hazards.

rw: An operating budget is a plan of expected revenues and expenses for day to day operations over a period, usually a year.

ww.A list of patients who are being treated: A list of current patients is a census, and it is not an operating budget, which is a financial plan of revenues and expenses.
ww.A plan to buy buildings and land for new: A plan to buy buildings and land is a capital budget, which covers large long term purchases, and it is not the operating budget.
ww.A schedule of staff shifts for the nurse: A shift schedule lists who works when and is not a financial plan, whereas an operating budget plans revenue and expenses for daily operations.

rw: A fixed cost does not change with patient volume, such as building rent, which a hospital pays whether it treats ten patients or ten thousand.

ww.Cost of medications per patient, which r: Medication cost per patient rises with each visit, so it varies with volume and is a variable cost, not a fixed one.
ww.Cost of meals per patient, which rises w: Meal cost per patient rises with every patient fed, so it varies with volume and is a variable cost, not a fixed one.
ww.Cost of bandages per patient, which rise: Bandage cost per patient rises with every patient treated, so it varies with volume and is a variable cost, not a fixed one.

rw: A variable cost changes with patient volume, such as medical supplies, which a hospital uses more of when it treats more patients.

ww.Building mortgage payments made each mon: Mortgage payments stay the same each month whatever the patient volume, so they are a fixed cost and not a variable one.
ww.Administrator salary paid each month to: A manager's salary stays the same each month whatever the patient numbers, so it is a fixed cost and not variable.
ww.Insurance premium for the building, fixe: An insurance premium on the building is fixed whatever the patient numbers, so it is a fixed cost and not a variable one.

rw: Total cost equals fixed cost plus variable cost, which is $50,000 plus $40 times 1,000 visits ($40,000), so the total is $90,000.

ww.$50,000: The $50,000 figure is only the fixed cost and leaves out the variable cost, which is $40 times 1,000 visits, or $40,000.
ww.$140,000: This answer is too high; the variable cost is $40 times 1,000 visits, equal to $40,000, so the total is $50,000 plus $40,000, which is $90,000.
ww.$40,000: The $40,000 figure is only the variable cost, which is $40 times 1,000 visits, and it leaves out the $50,000 of fixed costs.

rw: Each visit adds $120 minus $60, which is $60 of contribution margin, and dividing fixed costs of $60,000 by $60 gives break even at 1,000 visits.

ww.2,000 visits: Using 2,000 visits would divide $60,000 by $30, but the contribution per visit is $120 minus $60, or $60, which gives 1,000 visits.
ww.600 visits: Dividing $60,000 by $100 would give 600 visits, but contribution per visit is $60, not $100, so break even is $60,000 divided by $60, or 1,000.
ww.500 visits: Break even of 500 visits would need $120 of contribution per visit, but the variable cost reduces it to $60, so $60,000 divided by $60 gives 1,000 visits.

rw: Net patient revenue is revenue from patient care after contractual adjustments and discounts, so it reflects what the hospital actually expects to collect.

ww.Interest income that a hospital earns on: Interest income is a nonoperating earning and is not net patient revenue, which comes from patient care after adjustments and discounts.
ww.Gross charges, the full prices before an: Gross charges are the full list prices before discounts, whereas net patient revenue is what remains after contractual adjustments and discounts are subtracted.
ww.Donations that a hospital receives from: Donations are not payment for patient care, so they are not net patient revenue, which is what the hospital earns from care after adjustments.

rw: Charity care is care provided free or at reduced cost to patients who are unable to pay, based on financial need, and it is not billed as bad debt.

ww.Care for paying patients who have insura: Care for paying patients with insurance is ordinary billed care, not charity care, which is given free or at a reduced cost to those unable to pay.
ww.Care for staff only, given at no cost to: Care for staff at no cost is an employee benefit, not charity care, which is given free or reduced to patients who cannot pay.
ww.Cosmetic care such as surgery to change: Cosmetic care is an elective service for appearance and is not charity care, which is free or reduced cost care for patients unable to pay.

rw: Bad debt is the amount owed by patients who are able to pay but do not, unlike charity care, which is given to those unable to pay.

ww.Care provided free to patients who canno: Care provided free to patients who cannot pay is charity care, which is a different category than bad debt, where the patient could pay but does not.
ww.Donations given to the hospital by local: Donations are gifts given to the hospital and are income, not debts owed by patients, so they do not describe bad debt.
ww.Insurance payments made to a hospital fo: Insurance payments are revenue the hospital receives for care and not an unpaid patient debt, so they do not describe bad debt.

rw: Operating margin is operating income divided by operating revenue, expressed as a percent, and it shows how much of each revenue dollar remains as operating profit.

ww.Total cash held by the hospital in its a: Cash held in accounts is a measure of liquidity, whereas operating margin is a profitability ratio of operating income to operating revenue.
ww.Total debt owed by the hospital to its l: Debt owed to lenders is a liability on the balance sheet, whereas operating margin is a profitability ratio of operating income to operating revenue.
ww.Total assets held by the hospital on its: Total assets are what the hospital owns on its books, whereas operating margin is a profitability ratio of operating income to operating revenue.

rw: Operating margin equals operating income divided by operating revenue, so $10 million divided by $200 million equals 0.05, which is 5 percent.

ww.20%: Operating margin is $10 million divided by $200 million, which is 5 percent, so 20 percent would need operating income of $40 million.
ww.2%: Dividing $10 million by $200 million gives 0.05, which is 5 percent, so 2 percent would need operating income of only $4 million.
ww.50%: Fifty percent would need operating income of $100 million, but $10 million divided by $200 million is 5 percent, so this is far too high.

rw: A cost center is a department that incurs costs but does not directly generate revenue, such as housekeeping, administration or maintenance, which support the hospital's care services.

ww.A patient room in a hospital ward where: A patient room is a place for care, but a cost center is a department that incurs costs without directly generating revenue, such as housekeeping.
ww.A department that earns profit by billin: A department that earns profit by billing is a revenue center, which is the opposite of a cost center, which only incurs costs.
ww.A bank that holds the funds of a hospita: A bank holding funds and lending money is a financial institution, not a hospital department, so it is not a cost center.

rw: A revenue center is a department that generates income by billing for services, such as radiology, surgery or the laboratory.

ww.A storage room for supplies in the basem: A storage room for supplies is a physical place and not a department that earns income, which is what a revenue center is.
ww.A department that only costs money, such: A department that only costs money, such as housekeeping, is a cost center, which is the opposite of a revenue center that earns income.
ww.A waiting room where visitors sit while: A waiting room is a space for visitors and earns no income by itself, so it is not a revenue center.

rw: Variance analysis compares actual results to budgeted amounts to understand differences, helping managers see where spending or revenue strayed from plan and why.

ww.Counting patients who come to the hospit: Counting patients each day is a census or volume count, not variance analysis, which compares actual results with budgeted amounts to find differences.
ww.Ranking staff by their pay and years of: Ranking staff by pay and service is a human resources task, not variance analysis, which compares actual results with budgeted amounts to find differences.
ww.Reviewing menus for the meals that are s: Reviewing meal menus is a dietary task, not variance analysis, which compares actual results with budgeted amounts to find differences.

rw: The variance is $11,500 minus $10,000, or $1,500, and since actual supply cost was higher than budgeted, the variance is unfavorable.

ww.$0 favorable or not: A variance of $0 would mean actual equals budget, but actual spending was $11,500 against a budget of $10,000, so there is a difference.
ww.$21,500 unfavorable: The figure $21,500 adds budget and actual together, but variance is the difference, which is $11,500 minus $10,000, or $1,500.
ww.$1,500 favorable: Spending over budget is unfavorable, not favorable, because actual cost of $11,500 exceeded the $10,000 budget by $1,500.

rw: A full-time equivalent is a unit measuring staff hours that equals one full-time employee, so two half-time workers count as one FTE.

ww.A type of insurance that covers the staf: An FTE is a measure of staff hours, not an insurance type, so a type of insurance covering staff is wrong.
ww.A patient count taken on each ward at th: A patient count at the start of the day is a census, not an FTE, which measures staff hours.
ww.A fee for employees who join the hospita: A fee paid by new employees is not what FTE means, since FTE is a unit measuring staff hours equal to one full-time worker.

rw: Three employees at 20 hours each total 60 hours, and dividing 60 by a full-time week of 40 hours gives 1.5 FTEs.

ww.0.5 FTEs: Half an FTE would be a single 20 hour worker, but three employees at 20 hours each total 60 hours, which is 1.5 FTEs.
ww.3 FTEs: Three FTEs would need each of the three employees to work 40 hours, but each works only 20 hours, so the total is smaller.
ww.2 FTEs: Two FTEs would need 80 total hours, but three employees at 20 hours each give only 60 hours, which is 1.5 FTEs.

rw: Cost benefit analysis compares the costs of a decision with its expected benefits, so managers can judge whether the benefits are worth the costs.

ww.Counting patients who come in to the cli: Counting patients each day is a volume count, not cost benefit analysis, which compares the costs of a decision with its expected benefits.
ww.Setting prices only, with no thought of: Setting prices without considering costs or benefits ignores the comparison at the heart of cost benefit analysis, so it does not describe the method.
ww.Auditing records of the hospital and che: Auditing records for errors is a review of accuracy, not cost benefit analysis, which compares the costs of a decision with its expected benefits.

rw: Return on investment measures the gain from an investment relative to its cost, usually as a percent, so it shows how much return each dollar invested earns.

ww.The sales total of a firm in a full year: Annual sales total is revenue, not return on investment, which measures gain from an investment relative to the amount invested.
ww.The cost of equipment used in the plant: The cost of equipment is an expense or an investment amount, but ROI compares the gain from an investment with what it cost.
ww.The tax paid by a hospital in each year: Tax paid is an obligation to the government and not a measure of investment performance like ROI, which compares gain with cost.

rw: ROI is net gain divided by cost, so $500,000 minus $400,000 is $100,000, and $100,000 divided by $400,000 equals 0.25, or 25 percent.

ww.100%: A return of 100 percent would need a gain equal to the cost of $400,000, but the net gain is $500,000 minus $400,000, which is $100,000.
ww.125%: The 125 percent figure divides the $500,000 revenue by $400,000, but ROI uses net gain, which is $100,000 divided by $400,000, or 25 percent.
ww.80%: The 80 percent figure inverts the ratio by dividing $400,000 by $500,000, but ROI is the gain of $100,000 divided by the $400,000 cost, which is 25 percent.

rw: Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its useful life, so a piece of equipment bought now is expensed gradually across the years it is used.

ww.A loan from a bank that is repaid over t: A loan repaid over time is debt financing, not depreciation, which spreads the cost of an asset over its useful life.
ww.A patient fee charged for each visit to: A patient fee for each visit is a charge for service, not depreciation, which spreads the cost of an asset over its useful life.
ww.A tax paid on the sale of goods in a sho: A tax on the sale of goods is a sales tax, not depreciation, which spreads the cost of an asset over its useful life.

rw: A balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time, following the equation that assets equal liabilities plus equity.

ww.A patient list that names each person wh: A patient list names those treated on a ward, which is a census, not a balance sheet, which is a financial statement.
ww.A statement of cash flows showing the mo: A statement of cash flows shows money moving in and out over a period, not a snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity, which is the balance sheet.
ww.A statement of income showing the revenu: A statement of income shows revenue and costs over a year, not a snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity, which is the balance sheet.

rw: An income statement shows revenues and expenses over a period, resulting in net income, so it reports the profit or loss for that time.

ww.Assets held at one date, with debts and: Assets, debts and equity at one date are shown on the balance sheet, not the income statement, which reports revenues and expenses over a period.
ww.Cash balances only, held in the bank acc: Cash balances alone are not the income statement, which reports revenues and expenses and results in net income, not just the cash held in accounts.
ww.Patient counts for each ward on each day: Patient counts by ward are operating statistics, not financial results, so they are not what an income statement shows.

rw: A cash flow statement shows cash coming in and going out over a period, which tells a manager whether the hospital can pay its bills.

ww.Assets held at a date by the hospital: Assets held at a date appear on the balance sheet, not the cash flow statement, which tracks cash coming in and going out over a period.
ww.Net income only, for a single full year: Net income alone is on the income statement, whereas a cash flow statement tracks cash coming in and going out over a period.
ww.Staff counts for each ward on each day: Staff counts per ward are workforce data and not financial results, so they are not what a cash flow statement shows.

rw: Payer mix is the proportion of revenue from payers such as Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers, and it strongly affects how much a hospital earns.

ww.A mix of staff that a hospital uses on e: A mix of staff on each floor describes skill mix, not payer mix, which is the proportion of revenue from each type of payer.
ww.A blend of medicines that a pharmacy pre: A blend of medicines prepared by a pharmacy is called compounding, not payer mix, which is the proportion of revenue from each type of payer.
ww.A mix of departments that share the same: A mix of departments sharing a building describes the hospital's layout, not payer mix, which is the proportion of revenue from each type of payer.

rw: A favorable payer mix has a larger share of commercial payers, who usually reimburse more than government programs such as Medicare and Medicaid, so revenue is higher.

ww.Government pays the most for each servic: Government programs generally pay less than commercial insurers for the same service, so saying government pays the most is wrong.
ww.It increases costs only, with no gain in: A favorable payer mix raises income and does not just raise costs, because higher paying payers bring in more revenue for the same services.
ww.It has no effect on the money that a hos: Payer mix has a large effect on revenue, because payers reimburse at different rates, so it is false that it has no effect on income.

rw: A grant is money awarded to support a program or research that need not be repaid, usually by a government agency or foundation.

ww.An insurance premium paid by a member ea: An insurance premium is a regular payment to keep a plan active and is not a grant, which is money awarded that need not be repaid.
ww.A patient bill sent to a person after a: A patient bill requests payment for care, so it is not a grant, which is money awarded that need not be repaid.
ww.A bank loan that a hospital must repay w: A bank loan must be repaid with interest, whereas a grant is money awarded that need not be repaid, so the loan is not a grant.

rw: A bond issue is borrowing money from investors to finance major projects, such as new buildings, and the hospital repays the principal with interest.

ww.A gift from donors to a hospital to help: A gift from donors is philanthropy and does not need repayment, whereas a bond issue is borrowing from investors that must be repaid with interest.
ww.A tax rebate paid to a hospital by the s: A tax rebate from the state is a refund and is not borrowing, whereas a bond issue raises money from investors that must be repaid.
ww.A patient payment made at the desk befor: A patient payment at the desk is revenue for care, whereas a bond issue is borrowing from investors to finance major projects.

rw: The deductible is already met, so the patient pays 20 percent coinsurance on the covered $1,000 bill, which is 0.20 times $1,000, or $200.

ww.$1,000: A patient owing $1,000 would pay the whole bill, but the deductible is met, so the plan shares cost and the patient pays only 20 percent, or $200.
ww.$1,700: A figure of $1,700 would add the full bill to a new deductible, but the deductible is already paid, so the patient owes just 20 percent of $1,000, or $200.
ww.$800: A patient owing $800 is the insurer's 80 percent share of the $1,000 bill, but the patient pays the 20 percent coinsurance, which is $200.

rw: The insurer pays 80 percent of the allowed amount, which is 0.80 times $500, or $400, and the patient pays the remaining $100 as coinsurance.

ww.$500: The insurer does not pay the full $500, because the plan pays only 80 percent of the allowed amount, so the patient shares 20 percent.
ww.$80: The figure $80 treats 80 percent as a dollar amount, but 80 percent of $500 is 0.80 times $500, which equals $400.
ww.$100: A payment of $100 is the patient's 20 percent coinsurance share of $500, not the insurer's 80 percent share, which is $400.

rw: An in-network provider generally must write off the $100 difference between the $300 billed and the $200 allowed amount, as the contract requires.

ww.Cancel the claim and refuse care: Canceling the claim and refusing care is not required, since the provider agreed to accept the allowed amount and must adjust the balance instead of refusing care.
ww.Bill the insurer again for $100: Billing the insurer again for the $100 difference is wrong, because the insurer has set $200 as the allowed amount and will not pay more.
ww.Bill the patient the full $100: Billing the patient the $100 difference is balance billing, which an in-network contract generally forbids, since the provider accepted the allowed amount.

rw: The best next step is to verify the coverage dates and then either bill the patient or correct the insurance information, so payment can be collected properly.

ww.Write off the whole amount without check: Writing off the full amount without checking coverage gives up money that could be collected, so it is not the best next step.
ww.Resubmit the same claim many times until: Resubmitting the same claim many times without changes will produce the same denial and wastes time, so it does not solve a lapsed policy.
ww.Change the date of service to a date whe: Changing the date of service to match active coverage is falsifying a record and is billing fraud, so it must never be done.

rw: CPT codes describe the procedures and services performed by providers, such as office visits, surgeries and tests, and they tell insurers what was done for billing.

ww.The insurance plans that a patient holds: The insurance plans that a patient holds are described by payer and plan records, not CPT codes, which describe procedures and services performed.
ww.Diseases diagnosed in a patient by a doc: Diseases diagnosed are described by ICD-10 codes, not CPT codes, which describe procedures and services performed by providers.
ww.The locations of hospital wards and unit: Locations of hospital wards are not coded with CPT, which describes procedures and services performed by providers; place of service uses a separate code set.

rw: ICD-10 codes describe diagnoses and conditions, such as diabetes or a fractured wrist, and they tell insurers why the patient needed care.

ww.Procedures done by providers: Procedures done by providers are described by CPT codes, not ICD-10, which describes diagnoses and conditions.
ww.Hospital room prices: Hospital room prices are set in a charge master and are not described by ICD-10, which describes diagnoses and conditions.
ww.Drugs prescribed by a doctor: Prescribed drugs are identified by drug codes such as NDC numbers, not ICD-10, which describes diagnoses and conditions.
